title: Impact of digital inpatient diabetes care on well-being and treatment experience
summary:
Continuous tissue glucose monitoring via a sensor in the upper arm is already an established alternative to fingerstick blood glucose testing for many diabetes patients in outpatient care. The sensor measures tissue glucose every 1–5 minutes. The large amount of data makes it possible to predict the glucose trend for the next 15–30 minutes using trend arrows. This measurement method allows glucose trends to be described in detail. In inpatient care for patients with diabetes mellitus, glucose measurements are usually performed every six to eight hours by means of a blood test using a finger prick. These measurements only provide snapshots of glucose metabolism, and especially at night, neither patients nor the medical professionals caring for them have information about glucose status for several hours. In addition, both patients and nursing staff find blood tests time-consuming. 
Digital diabetes management can improve the care and treatment of patients with diabetes mellitus. The digital system measures tissue glucose levels via the sensor and transmits them to the patient's device (smartphone with corresponding app). From there, the data is transferred to a tablet with a corresponding app, where it can be viewed by healthcare professionals, allowing them to monitor the patient at all times.
This advanced therapy and treatment of diabetes mellitus using technological advances requires special skills and knowledge from both patients and healthcare professionals. Digital diabetes management could therefore have positive effects for patients and healthcare professionals in terms of problem areas in diabetes treatment and workload, digital literacy, and satisfaction with the treatment process.
